content: Lung cancer, also known as pulmonary carcinoma, is a malignant tumor arising from the tissues of the lungs. It primarily develops when lung cells undergo genetic mutations leading to uncontrolled growth. The two main types are non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), comprising approximately 85% of cases, and small cell lung cancer (SCLC). Major risk factors include tobacco smoking, exposure to radon gas, asbestos, air pollution, and genetic predisposition. Symptoms often emerge in later stages and include persistent cough, hemoptysis (coughing blood), chest pain, and unexplained weight loss. Diagnosis relies on imaging tests such as chest X-rays and CT scans, followed by tissue biopsy for histological confirmation. Treatment options vary based on the cancer stage and type and include surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, targeted biological agents, and immunotherapy. Early detection improves prognosis but remains challenging due to nonspecific symptoms. Lifestyle modifications, especially smoking cessation, significantly reduce risk and improve treatment outcomes. Despite advances, lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer-related death worldwide. Understanding mechanisms, proper evaluation, and safety considerations in management are critical for patient care and public health. Synonyms like pulmonary neoplasm are less commonly used in lay contexts. Limitations in current knowledge include variability in treatment responses and ongoing research in molecular targeted therapies. Safety concerns emphasize the need to manage treatment side effects and minimize exposure to carcinogens.

chunk_title: Definition and Types of Lung Cancer
content: Lung cancer is a malignant tumor originating from the epithelial cells of the lung airways or alveoli. Major types include non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), which makes up about 85% of cases and includes subtypes like adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and large cell carcinoma. Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) is more aggressive and accounts for roughly 15%. These classifications guide treatment decisions and prognosis.

content: The leading cause of lung cancer is tobacco smoking, responsible for approximately 85% of cases. Other causes include long-term exposure to radon gas, asbestos, air pollution, secondhand smoke, and occupational carcinogens. Genetic susceptibility and family history also influence risk. Notably, never-smokers can develop lung cancer, often linked to specific genetic mutations.

content: Lung cancer develops when genetic mutations in lung cells disrupt normal cell cycle regulation, enabling uncontrolled proliferation. Key molecular pathways involved include mutations in the EGFR gene, KRAS gene, and ALK rearrangements. These molecular changes contribute to tumor initiation, growth, angiogenesis, and metastasis.

content: Early lung cancer often causes no symptoms. When symptoms appear, they may include a persistent cough, blood-tinged sputum (hemoptysis), chest pain, shortness of breath, recurrent respiratory infections, hoarseness, unexplained weight loss, and fatigue. Symptoms arise due to tumor growth obstructing airways or invading adjacent structures.

content: Diagnosis involves initial imaging like chest X-ray and computed tomography (CT) scans to identify suspicious lung masses. Positron emission tomography (PET) may assess metabolic activity and staging. Confirmatory diagnosis requires tissue biopsy obtained via bronchoscopy, needle aspiration, or surgery. Laboratory tests and molecular profiling guide treatment planning.

content: Treatment depends on cancer type, stage, patient health, and molecular characteristics. Early-stage NSCLC may be treated surgically. Chemotherapy and radiation therapy are standard for many stages. Targeted therapies (e.g., EGFR inhibitors) and immunotherapy have transformed management of certain molecular subtypes, improving survival. SCLC often requires combination chemotherapy and radiation due to rapid progression.

content: Lung cancer prognosis varies by stage and type. Five-year survival rates for localized NSCLC can exceed 60%, but overall rates remain below 20% due to late diagnosis. SCLC has a poorer prognosis because of its aggressive nature. Early detection and advances in personalized therapy are improving outcomes gradually.

content: Avoiding smoking is the most effective prevention strategy. Reducing exposure to radon and occupational carcinogens, improving air quality, and adopting a healthy lifestyle with balanced nutrition and physical activity support lung health. Smoking cessation during and after diagnosis improves treatment response and quality of life.

content: Treatments can cause side effects like fatigue, nausea, organ toxicity, and immune-related reactions. Managing these safely requires monitoring and supportive care.
